_world_state.title: World State (Canonical Bullets)
_world_state.content:
World Snapshot
Qualihut lies under the paper-sovereignty of the Divine Elvish Empire: a sprawling feudal machine that claims everything in ink and controls far less in practice. Power travels by courier, contract, and caravan; most people feel “the Empire” as taxes, tolls, and the sudden arrival of someone with a seal.
Magic is real, finite, and increasingly processed into something portable and tradable. The result is a world where spellcraft has a price tag and a custody chain—and where money can literally flare in your hands when you try to redeem it.
Travel is dangerous by default. Old-growth forests are protected and politically touchy; the central wilds refuse to stay mapped; the Three-Moon Sea is unstable under three moons. Those who gamble on the Fey Roads can cross impossible distances, but time and memory do not always come back in the same shape.
Time is negotiated. The Empire keeps calendars and census clocks; the Fey do not. Gods are present in the way storms are present—felt, argued about, never wholly trusted. The dead do not come back by default; if a return happens at all, it is a cost, a condition, or a story.
Current Pressures (Player-Facing)

In Hochsilvar, guild power rises and court power turns defensive; decisions feel financial before they feel moral.
The Banking Guild is teaching people to treat paper like law—until a ledger hiccups and a riot starts looking like “market correction.”
The Southern Union smiles through treaties and keeps everyone guessing whether the next insult arrives as a speech, a bribe, or a fire.
Sea routes migrate under three moons; caravans become targets; “safe passage” is leverage sold twice.
The Fey Roads tempt the desperate with impossible distance, and collect their fee in time, memory, and aftermath.

Campaign Frame (Player-Facing)

You begin as competent professionals, assembled into a new team under the Empire’s long-view bureaucracy (Der Weitblick) and its cut-outs.
Expect covert work, leverage, and bureaucracy: maps, ledgers, favors, and deniable violence.
The world is a sandbox; choices move factions and change the map.
Magic is high-impact but not free; it has markets, custody chains, and consequences.
Death is meaningful; replacement characters enter through the same apparatus.

briefings/banco-valdieri-investigation.title: Banco Valdieri Investigation
briefings/banco-valdieri-investigation.content:
Briefing: Banco Valdieri Investigation
Distribution
Joint Task Force personnel only. Do not copy. Do not annotate. Do not discuss outside authorized rooms.
Situation summary
Banco Valdieri has suffered a major theft of refined magic jars. This threatens public confidence in the Banking Guild’s promissory-note system and, by extension, the calm the Crown is selling to the city.
This occurs during The Royal Games (solstice week). Hochsilvar is overcrowded: rival supporters roam drunk and loud, cargo traffic surges, and every empty bed is already occupied. Expect delays, distractions, and incidents that look “random” until they don’t.
The City Watch has established a three-day magical quarantine while forensic wizards examine the scene. Expect rumors, opportunists, and attempts to seize control of the narrative masquerading as “help.”
This matter is politically sensitive. The Banking Guild is demanding results. The Crown expects calm.
Your status and authority
You are assigned to a Joint Task Force comprised of:

Hochsilvar City Watch (scene control, arrests, public order)
Der Kronenschild (domestic intelligence arm; authorized by agreement with the Crown to operate across the feudal states)

You are expected to:

coordinate with the City Watch, not fight them,
minimize public disturbance,
keep the Banking Guild cooperative without allowing them to seize control of the investigation,
produce actionable leads within the quarantine window.

Quarantine rules (effective immediately)

The crime scene perimeter is controlled by the City Watch.
No personnel may enter the perimeter carrying magical items. Violations will be confiscated and logged.
Divinations and active spellwork inside the perimeter require the Watch forensics team’s approval.
Quarantine is scheduled for 3 days, extendable at the Watch’s discretion.

Known facts

The vault and its mechanisms show anomalous arcane interference consistent with a sophisticated breach.
Initial witness accounts contain inconsistencies in timing and sequence.
Banco Valdieri’s owner and ward staff are conducting their own internal review under Banking Guild pressure.
The incident occurred at noon on the solstice (Royal Games week), when the city’s attention is split and crowds provide natural cover.

Immediate tasks

Report to Captain Ensio Silbermark for access protocols and the current forensics schedule.
Secure and review Banco Valdieri’s public-facing records relevant to custody-chain and promissory-note exposure.
Establish a preliminary list of personnel with vault access, including emergency procedures and watch rotations.
Identify any external pressures already being applied (guild militia presence, legal representatives, court couriers).

Conduct expectations

Keep your cover clean. You are here as the Crown’s domestic stability partner, not as an independent power.
Avoid unnecessary violence. Avoid public scenes. Avoid creating martyrs.
If you must break a rule to obtain a lead, be prepared to explain the political cost.

briefings/character-creation-and-table-r.title: Character Creation + Table Rules
briefings/character-creation-and-table-r.content:
Character creation (player-safe)
This is the shared baseline for building characters and avoiding rules surprises. If something here doesn’t fit what you want to play, talk to the GM early—this setting supports customization, but it does so by making choices consequential.
System + materials

System: D&D (2024 core rules)
Character options: core rules by default, with additional options by table agreement (no 3rd-party/homebrew without a quick review).

Allowed ancestries (default)

Human / Half-elf / Elf / Half-orc are the assumed “normal” mix for PCs.
Other ancestries exist in the world, but are opt-in with table agreement so they fit tone and don’t step on mysteries.

Classes are social
Any class can work here; what matters is where your power comes from and what it costs socially.

Clerics/paladins: faith is real, but institutions have pressure and politics.
Wizards/“trained mages”: entangled with gatekeeping, custody chains, and markets.
Sorcerers: talent and bloodline attention (good and bad).
Warlocks: restricted—by default, warlock PCs must have a credible tie to House von Stillwort and its patron, The Silent Poet.
Rogues/bards/rangers: thrive in a world of borders, leverage, and dangerous travel.

Subclass notes (current)

Bards: default PC colleges are Lore or Dance. Fey bards are NPC-facing; College of Glamour is not available for PCs. College of Valor is not used for PCs.

Campaign contract (table expectations)

You are competent adults; you can be compromised, but not a joke character.
You are expected to work as a team (shared risk, shared cover).
Secrets are welcome; sabotage and PvP require consent.

Rules (from the Session Zero recording)

Ruleset (current baseline): D&D 2024 core rules.
Session zero originally referenced “core rules / Expanded 2014”; treat that as historical and superseded.
Advancement: milestone (for now).
Starting level: 3
Ability scores: roll 3d6 + 3; reroll 1s; generate 6 stats and then assign; reroll the full set if unhappy.
Background ability score increases: ignored.
Ancestry bonuses: only explicitly called out is orc +2 INT.
Skills: +5 discretionary points across a short list (Deception, Insight, Intimidation, Investigation, Perception, Persuasion, Sleight of Hand, Stealth).
HP: either roll or take average per level.
Spells: curated/approved spell list. Current bans: Goodberry, Find Traps, Knock, Prestidigitation, Protection from Evil and Good.
Renamed spells (table terminology): Fox Fire (Faerie Fire), Fiery Rebuke (Hellish Rebuke), Animal Omen (Augury).
Explicitly ok: Pass Without Trace.
Starting gear: standard issue “assassin’s dagger” / returning dagger (in addition to normal gear).
Units: prefer metric (meters) at the table.

Still TBD / confirm in writing

Allowed subclasses and multiclassing policy (“you’ve got to pay”).
Rest model: Safe haven long rests (locked).

Rest model options (what these mean)

RAW (default 5e pacing): short rest is about 1 hour; long rest is about 8 hours. Best if you want more frequent “reset” and more heroic day-to-day endurance.
Safe haven long rests: short rests work normally, but long rests only count in truly safe places (e.g., an inn you trust, a secured barracks, a friendly house, a warded camp with permission). Best if you want travel to stay dangerous without rewriting the whole system.
Creating safe havens in the wild is possible (and expected) if the party has the skills, time, and cover to secure a site. The GM adjudicates what counts as “safe.”
Gritty realism: short rest is about 8 hours; long rest is about 7 days. Best if you want injury/exhaustion to matter and downtime to be part of play; can be rough on classes balanced around short rests.

Prompts (quick hooks that fit the setting)
Pick 2–3:

Who do you owe, and what kind of “receipt” do they keep?
What border did you cross the official way and the unofficial way?
What scarce thing are you good at (navigation, seals, wards, healing, languages, accounting)?
What did you lose time to (a road, a storm, a fever, a bargain)?

Player-safe reading (optional)

Play Contract + Working Agreements
World Briefing (Player Teaser)
World State (Canonical Bullets)
Magic Briefing (Player)

briefings/creation-myth-sun-moon-forest.title: Creation Myth: Sun, Moon, Forest (and the Fey Lord Who Chuckled)
briefings/creation-myth-sun-moon-forest.content:
The Telling (common, player-safe)
Before there was earth, there was Light and Growth.
Althar, the Sun, burned without form: endless, unrooted, unable to hold what it revealed. Waldrun, the Forest, spread without warmth: potential without motion, life that could not wake.
They did not rule. They recognized one another. And in that recognition, they made the world.
The First Seed
The Forest shaped the first seed and placed it where the Sun could see it. The Sun did not command it to grow. He waited.
When light and root met correctly, the seed split—not into a plant, but into Being. From it emerged the Wife of the Sun: fertility without chaos, growth with rhythm, life that could repeat. Where she walked, the earth became habitable.
The Birth of Night (and the Three Moons)
When she emerged, the world brightened too quickly. Life surged. Heat lingered. Nothing rested.
So the Wife turned to the darkness beyond the world and shaped it. From that shaping came three moons—not one, never one—known in later tellings as Elunara’s threefold face, to govern what the Sun cannot:

one moon rules rest and sleep
one moon rules cycles, blood, and birth
one moon rules memory, death, and return

The Sun illuminates truth. The moons make truth survivable.
The Forest’s Place
The Forest did not retreat. It remained: older than cities, patient beyond kings, witness to every cycle. It is not ruled by the Sun; it negotiates through seasons, decay, and regrowth.
This is why druids whisper: darkness is not evil—it is regulation; life that never rests becomes catastrophe.
The Fey Lord Who Chuckled
And the Fey Lord looked upon what they had made—light with purpose, growth with rhythm, moons set to keep the dark from swallowing the living—and chuckled. In some tellings, the name of that sovereign is Caernlach.
Not in mockery. In recognition. The story says the Fey did not undo creation. They tilted it: bent distance, time, and certainty, just enough to keep the world alive.
The old Fey saying is rarely translated the same way twice, but the sense is consistent:
Not to ruin the music.
To keep it alive.
The old line that closes the telling is usually spoken, not sung:
“The Sun teaches us when to grow.
The Forest teaches us when to stop.”
Sometimes the telling adds:
“The Sun gives life meaning.
The Forest gives life patience.
The Moons make life possible.”
The story says that laughter fell into the cracks between Sun-law, Moon-rhythm, and Forest-memory. It became thresholds: paths that fold, hours that slip, and names that don’t fit the same way twice.
How people use this story

The Solar Church tells it as a warning: growth requires discipline, and discipline requires obedience.
Forest folk tell it as a reminder: take only what you can repay, and leave the land able to answer tomorrow.
Rangers repeat the last line before they camp: if the pattern breaks, keep moving.

See also

The Three-Moon Sea
Old-Growth Forests
The Fey Roads
The Three Moons
The Solar Church
Althar
Elunara
Waldrun
Skaldren

briefings/druid-briefing-player.title: Druid Briefing (Player)
briefings/druid-briefing-player.content:
Player briefing: Druids in Qualihut (player-safe)
Druids in Qualihut treat magic like ecology: something you listen to, negotiate with, and pay for later. They care less about “power” and more about cycle discipline: when to grow, when to stop, when to burn, when to remember.
If you play (or travel with) a druid, you’ll see a few repeated habits:

Watching the sky like sailors watch weather.
Treating boundaries (groves, seasons, oaths) as real constraints, not vibes.
Recording what matters in bodies and living memory, not in books.

The Three Moons (the sky as a pressure system)
Most druids track nights the way merchants track prices: not for poetry, but because it changes what the world will tolerate.

Canon overview: The Three Moons

At the table, you can use this as roleplay texture:

One moon makes rest come easily (or makes sleep dangerous).
One moon makes blood and growth behave strangely (generous or brittle).
One moon makes memory, endings, and “return” feel close (clean or contaminated).

The Living Script (druid memory that can burn)
Some druid circles don’t trust paper to keep faith. They keep record in living bodies: tattoos as archive, rank, oath, grief, and proof.

Player-safe details: The Living Script

Magical tattoo ink (spellwork done through skin)
Not every tattoo is “Script.” Some tattoos are spellcraft: a working bound to flesh, harder to steal and harder to remove.

Player-safe details: Magical Tattoo Ink

Common rumors

Elder druids can be “read” the way priests read scripture, if you know the practice.
The best ink costs more than steel, and the worst ink leaves scars that still “itch” when magic is near.
On certain moon-nights, tattoos look like they’re remembering something you aren’t.

See also

Creation Myth: Sun, Moon, Forest
The Three-Moon Sea

briefings/gender-fluidity.title: Gender, Orientation, and Shamans
briefings/gender-fluidity.content:
Gender and orientation (player-safe)
In Qualihut, there is no stigma attached to gender fluidity, transness, or sexual orientation. People notice presentation the way they notice regional accents or guild rings: as information, not as a moral category.
This is partly cultural and partly institutional: the Solar Church is a legitimacy machine (calendars, witnesses, contracts, heir-records), not an afterlife-policing religion. There is no heaven or hell in the way some faiths argue about, so the Church has no doctrinal need to legislate private life as “sin” in exchange for promised salvation.
Shamans (common and unremarkable)
Many spirit negotiators and rural ritual specialists (often called “shamans” in common speech) are gender fluid. In-world, this is treated as normal: a social flexibility that fits a job defined by mediation, thresholds, and speaking across categories.
At the table

Gender and orientation are not a “gotcha,” a joke axis, or a stigma engine in this campaign.
If you want a personal arc about identity, it is welcome, but it will be framed as your character’s life, not as society’s default cruelty.

briefings/magic-briefing-player.title: Magic Briefing (Player)
briefings/magic-briefing-player.content:
Player briefing: how magic works (what your character can know)
In Qualihut, magic is real, useful, and never free.
Two things matter more than spell lists:

Magic behaves like a finite resource you can refine, trade, and corrupt.
Time is not universal: consensus time exists; Fey time does not.

The everyday reality

Most “magic” people experience is practical: wards on gates, blessings on contracts, rituals that keep a town’s water clean, and small protections that prevent a bad season from becoming a riot.
Big magic exists, but it concentrates around institutions (guilds, churches, courts) and along dangerous routes (wilds, sea lanes, thresholds).

Refined magic (money that can explode)

Refined magic is power made portable—used like fuel, like currency, and like ordnance.
It’s traded through seals, audits, and custody chains. If you touch it, you become interesting.

Divine magic (miracles with bureaucracy)

People pray because it helps. Priests also perform sanctioned rites that sometimes produce real effects.
Those rites come with calendars, witnesses, and paperwork. The holy has logistics.

Mind magic (used judiciously) + wards

In the Empire, “mind magic” (charms, compulsions, emotional manipulation) is treated like a kind of quiet assault: useful, feared, and socially expensive when discovered.
Wards against mind magic are widely available, and even cheap wards can make manipulation noticeable.
Player-safe details (what it feels like, how wards work, and what to expect in play): Mind Magic + Wards

Nature and liminal magic (roads, forests, thresholds)

Druids and old practitioners treat magic like an ecology: listen, align, pay costs later.
Thresholds and “thin places” can bend time, memory, and causality. Travel is dangerous because the world has teeth.

What to assume as a player

If a situation feels neat, someone is lying—or someone else already paid the cost.
Magic solves problems and creates second-order problems immediately.

briefings/play-contract.title: Play Contract + Working Agreements
briefings/play-contract.content:
Play contract (player-safe)
This campaign runs best when everyone shares expectations about tone, teamwork, and how secrets work. This is that agreement.
Tone & themes

Wonder and dread.
Political absurdity.
Scarcity and trade pressure.
Secrets with consequences (not secrets as “gotchas”).

What play looks like

You begin as competent professionals, assembled into a new team under imperial bureaucracy and its cut-outs.
Expect covert work, leverage, and paperwork: maps, ledgers, favors, and deniable violence.
The world is a sandbox; choices move factions and change the map.
Travel is dangerous by default; “routine long-distance travel” is a lie people tell to sell tickets.
Magic is high-impact but not free; it has markets, custody chains, and second-order effects.
Death is meaningful; treat resurrection as rare/conditional at best, not a build assumption.

Party expectations

Build a character who wants to work with the group (shared risk, shared cover).
Chase leads and make calls with incomplete information; the world won’t wait for perfect certainty.
Expect tradeoffs: you rarely get a clean win and a clean conscience.

Secrets, conflict, and consent

No player-to-player secrets: we keep everything open OOC; any secrecy is character-context only.
Character secrets are welcome when they create future decisions, not table sabotage.
No one uses secrets to remove another player’s agency without consent.
Sabotage and PvP require explicit consent at the table (narrative conflict is fine; surprise mechanical betrayal is not).

Safety & boundaries
The setting includes political cruelty, scarcity pressure, and moral compromise. We set clear boundaries in session zero and play within them.

briefings/world-briefing-player-teaser.title: World Briefing (Player Teaser)
briefings/world-briefing-player-teaser.content:
Qualihut: A World Briefing (Player-Safe)
Ink is the Empire’s first weapon.
They call it the Divine Elvish Empire, a sprawling feudal machine that claims whole regions with seals and signatures, then spends the next century discovering that maps don’t obey paperwork. In most towns, “the Empire” arrives as taxes, tolls, and sudden couriers bearing a stamped demand—someone, somewhere, has decided you belong to a ledger now.
Power moves the same way: by courier, contract, and caravan. A noble’s decree is only as real as the riders who carry it. A guild’s promise is only as strong as the hands that witness it. When people speak of law, they mean the ability to enforce it without burning the world down in the process.
That tension—between what is claimed and what is controlled—is where Qualihut lives.
Magic, Made Portable
Magic is real. It is also finite, tradable, and increasingly processed into something portable: refined magic, sealed into containers and moved like currency.
In the great cities, finance is becoming ritual. The Banking Guild offers promissory notes backed by vaults, seals, and witnessed redemption. Paper begins to behave like law. Merchants stop weighing coin and start weighing reputation. And when a ledger hiccups, a crowd can turn hungry fast—because the money in their hands is no longer just metal. It can flare, fail, or betray them.
To spellcasters, refined magic is fuel: a way to push a casting beyond ordinary limits. To everyone else, it’s gold and gunpowder at the same time—valuable, dangerous, and worth killing for.
The World Does Not Travel Kindly
In Qualihut, travel is never “routine.” It is a decision you make with your life.
The Three-Moon Sea is not a road. With three moons tugging at the world, tides argue with each other, currents migrate, and “safe passage” is never permanent—only negotiated. Old charts get people killed because they encourage confidence. Monsters treat shipping lanes like feeding corridors. Ports survive on conditional knowledge: this channel is passable this month, at this moonrise, if your captain knows the signs and your crew can stomach what they’ll see when the water decides to misbehave.
Inland, old-growth forests are not wilderness so much as politics. Wood is scarce where it matters, and logging is trouble—legal trouble, religious trouble, and sometimes the kind of trouble that has no paperwork. Shrines appear where roads don’t, and certain groves are treated like borders: you can cross them, but only if you accept that you are being noticed.
And then there is the desert.
The desert is not empty. It is unstable. Water does not “run” here; it relocates. Oases appear, vanish, and migrate as if the land is changing its mind. A good map is a story you can trade, not a truth you can trust. Caravans survive by treating the road as law: how you take water, what you leave behind, and whether you keep your word when the map stops caring.
Roads That Aren’t Roads
Fast travel exists—if you are willing to bargain with a world that does not experience time the way you do.
The Fey Roads are liminal paths where distance stops behaving, time slips its leash, and the world feels like it’s being negotiated rather than inhabited. People speak of “missing time” the way sailors speak of storms: not as a metaphor, but as a debt. You can cross impossible distances, and return with memory-holes you cannot name, or a week you cannot account for, or an aftermath you didn’t earn but now have to live with.
Most sane folk avoid the Fey Roads. Those who can’t—spies, desperate merchants, pilgrims chasing miracles—do it with rituals, bargains, and guides who never quite answer questions directly.
Faith, Authority, and the Price of Being Wrong
The Empire keeps calendars and census clocks. The Fey do not. Time is negotiated.
Gods are present in the way storms are present—felt, argued about, never wholly trusted. People pray because it helps, because it might matter, because it’s what you do when the world is bigger than you. But no one sensible builds a plan that depends on divine certainty arriving on schedule.
Death is meaningful. The dead do not come back by default. If a return happens at all, it is a cost, a condition, or a story—and stories always want something.
Where You Fit In
Qualihut is a world of leverage: a stamped document that can move a caravan, a jar that can buy a city’s loyalty, a rumor that can start a war without a single banner raised.
In the capital of Hochsilvar, court power turns defensive while guild power rises—decisions feel financial before they feel moral. At border cities like Valdengratz, passage is a market as much as it is a line: everyone sells something, whether it’s legitimacy, silence, or a stamped lid.
And beyond the cities, the map is never finished. The wilds refuse to stay mapped. Sea routes migrate. Oases move. The Fey Roads whisper. The Empire claims, the world resists, and people adapt—ingeniously, ruthlessly, and often beautifully.
Who You Can Be (Ancestry & Class)
Ancestries (common and playable)
In this campaign’s core assumptions, the “ordinary” mix is shaped by the Empire: humans and half-elves in the streets, elves in the archives and courts, and orcs wherever trade needs muscle, mediation, or someone who can speak to three different kinds of trouble in a single afternoon.

Human / Half-elf: the Empire’s majority reality—local loyalties, hard compromises, and a life lived under paperwork that arrives from far away.
Elf: long-lived stewards of archives, forests, and heraldry; patient, political, and difficult to rush.
Orc: fully woven into society as caravan guards, dock muscle, negotiators, and fixers—common enough to be unremarkable and networked enough to be dangerous to underestimate.

Other beings exist in the world—things tied to hot volcanic corridors, predatory symbiotes, and the Fey themselves—but they are rare, risky, and not assumed as standard player options unless we agree on it together.
Classes (how they fit the world)
Any class can work in Qualihut. What matters is where your power comes from and what it costs you socially.

Clerics and paladins are taken seriously, but not always trusted; faith is real here, and so is institutional pressure.
Wizards and artificers (or any “trained mage” concept) are entangled with markets, custody chains, and professional gatekeeping; magic is a discipline and a commodity.
Sorcerers tend to attract stories: envy, fear, and people who want to make your talent someone else’s asset.
Warlocks fit perfectly, because bargains fit perfectly; just remember that a shortcut that bends distance and time is still a debt.
Rogues, bards, and rangers thrive in a world where travel is leverage, borders are markets, and information moves faster than armies.
Druids and barbarians exist at the edges—forests, wilds, deserts, coastlines—where “civilization” is a rumor the land hasn’t agreed to yet.

Recruitment Info (Player-Facing)
What you’ll do
You’ll take jobs where the clean version is “investigation” and the true version is “leverage”: untangling who benefits, moving through borders and paperwork, making deals you can survive, and choosing which fires get to burn.
Expect a mix of:

faction politics and hard choices
travel as an adventure (and a risk), not a montage
social play, negotiation, and consequences that persist
occasional violence that is fast, messy, and never free

Character hooks (choose one or two)

You owe someone who keeps receipts (a guild, a temple, a patron, a crew).
You’ve crossed a border the official way and the unofficial way, and you learned what each costs.
You’ve lost time to a road, a storm, a fever, or a bargain—and you don’t fully trust your own timeline.
You’re good at a scarce thing (navigation, seals, wards, healing, languages, accounting) and people keep trying to turn it into ownership.

Table expectations
This campaign runs best with characters who:

want to work as a team (shared risk, shared cover)
will chase leads and make calls with incomplete information
can live with tradeoffs (you rarely get a clean win and a clean conscience)

Safety & tone
The setting has political cruelty, scarcity pressure, and moral compromise. We’ll set clear boundaries in session zero and play within them.
Allowed options (default)

Core playable ancestries: human/half-elf, elf, orc.
Anything else (rare ancestries, unusual origins) is opt-in with table agreement so it fits the tone and doesn’t spoil mysteries.

If you’re looking for a setting where wonder has teeth, where politics is personal, where magic has consequences, and where every shortcut charges interest, you’ve found it.

What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

In the deep desert, there are stands of fast-growing “bamboo trees” that appear where water briefly agrees to exist. They are not forests. They are episodes: a sudden flare of green that becomes poles, shade ribs, tools, fuel, and then—often—vanishes as the land shifts again.
Caravan folk treat these groves like a blessing and a warning. You can build a camp from them, but you can’t build permanence. If you try, the desert collects your effort as scrap.
Common rumors

These groves “know where water is” before scouts do.
Some seasonal truffles form on their roots, and that fact makes people with titles unusually polite to people without them.

See also

The Desert (Living System)
Desert Truffle

economy/desert-truffle.title: Desert Truffle
economy/desert-truffle.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

In polite church and court talk, “the desert truffle” or more ritually, “Sun-Blood” is rare, seasonal, and never discussed at full volume. It is said to grow only when the desert’s hidden water and heat happen to agree, and to spoil if handled by people who don’t know the road.
Most folk will never see one. What they see instead are the consequences: caravans delayed for “calendar reasons,” church custody tightening, and the sudden seriousness of officials who pretend belief is optional.
Common rumors

A late truffle season causes panic in places that pretend to be rational.
The truffle can’t be farmed; it can only be found—and only by those who know how the desert moves.
Some Travelers can smell the season the way sailors smell storms.

See also

The Travelers
Desert Bamboo (Fast-Growth Trees)
The Desert (Living System)
Sacrament Administration
Church Caravans

economy/distilled-elf-flower-wine.title: Distilled Elf Flower Wine
economy/distilled-elf-flower-wine.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Distilled elf flower wine is a rare, highly concentrated spirit made from elven
flower vintages. Most people treat it as rumor: too expensive, too dangerous,
and too specific to be ordinary tavern vice.
In undercity speech, it is usually called Dream Wine or Silent Clarity.
Common rumors

A measured dose can make someone move “one heartbeat ahead” of everyone else.
Counterfeit bottles are more common than real ones and kill faster.

See also

Pitcher Sap

economy/druidic-endurance-leaf.title: Druidic Endurance Leaf
economy/druidic-endurance-leaf.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Druidic endurance leaf is a bitter chew used by hunters, messengers, field
laborers, and caravan walkers to push through long effort without collapsing.
It is practical, unglamorous, and common in rural exchange.
Street names include Longwalk, Stonebite, and Workleaf.
Common rumors

City people mock leaf-chewers until they need one on the road.
Good leaf smells grassy and sharp; bad leaf smells sweet and wrong.

See also

Distilled Elf Flower Wine

economy/fish-farming.title: Fish Farming
economy/fish-farming.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

In river deltas, monastery ponds, and sheltered coastal pens, fish are raised the way grain is raised: patiently, in rows and fences you can’t see until you’re already trespassing. In lean years, fish keeps cities fed without the same public blood-and-ritual politics as herd slaughter.
If you want to understand who holds power in a “quiet” town, don’t count swords—count sluice gates, weirs, and the keys to pond locks. Water rights decide who eats, who sells, and who suddenly finds their nets cut.
Common rumors

Monasteries can “bless” a pond so the fish breed true, even in bad water.
Some guilds would rather pay bandits than pay a canal inspector.

economy/hideleaf.title: Hideleaf (Plant Leather)
economy/hideleaf.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Hideleaf is “peasant leather”: thick green leaves cured until they’re tough enough for boots, aprons, and work coats. New hideleaf smells like limewater and bark tea, and it creases like stubborn paper until it learns your stride.
In the countryside it’s a blessing—shoes without slaughter. In cities it’s an argument. Some tanners and leatherworkers treat it as an insult to their craft; others buy it in bulk for armies and caravans because it’s cheap, durable, and doesn’t ask questions.
Common rumors

A man in hideleaf is either poor, practical, or lying about being both.
Hideleaf boots last longer if you oil them with fish fat (and they smell like it).

See also

The Central Wilds

economy/insect-spice.title: Insect Spice (Borrowed Heat)
economy/insect-spice.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

“Spice” in many markets isn’t a far-off flower or a noble’s imported powder—it’s insect heat: dried, crushed compounds taken from things that sting, bite, or burn predators for a living. Cooks call it borrowed heat; priests call it a test of the body’s honesty.
Most households keep mild blends for preservation and parasite-killing. The truly fierce powders—slow-bloom reds, sharp green flashes, black pepper that makes your ears ring—are status, dare, and sometimes medicine. Spice sellers are part gourmand, part apothecary, and they’ll watch you taste like they’re reading a confession.
Common rumors

The best spice comes from insects that only feed on yellow grass during the height of summer.
Some “spice” isn’t heat at all—just a joy that makes you forget the hour.

economy/marsh-dyed-textiles.title: Marsh-Dyed Textiles
economy/marsh-dyed-textiles.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Marsh-dyed textiles are one of the best-known exports of
The River Marches: supple river-silk and
reed-cloth worked into garments and bolts whose muted colors shift like wet
stone, old bronze, moss, or storm water depending on the light.
Common rumors

Courtiers wear Marcher cloth and pretend not to notice where it comes from.
The best patterns mean something; cheap copies only look expensive.

See also

The River Marches
Statesboro

economy/pitcher-sap.title: Pitcher Sap
economy/pitcher-sap.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Pitcher sap is a jungle-harvested intoxicant resin traded in tiny vials and
leaf wraps. It is prized for confidence and feared for the same reason.
Street names include Green Joy, Cupblood, and Laughing Resin.
Common rumors

A strong batch makes fear feel optional.
Most people who boast about handling sap are lying or dead.

See also

Distilled Elf Flower Wine

economy/pottery-and-seals.title: Pottery, Kilns, and Trade Seals
economy/pottery-and-seals.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

In the Empire, clay is bureaucracy you can hold. Goods travel in stamped jars, not just because barrels are expensive, but because a seal makes a thing “real” to the law. If it fits in a vessel with the right mark, it can be taxed, insured, requisitioned, or confiscated.
Market stalls keep stacks of broken lids and shards the way richer folk keep receipts—proof that you paid, proof that you were allowed to have it. Inspectors press seals, tap rims, and stare at clay like it might lie. Sometimes it does.
Common rumors

A forged kiln-stamp buys you entry to the city… until someone checks the year mark.
Wars are won by kilns and clerks as often as by knights.

economy/salt-pork.title: Salt Pork (Jar Trade)
economy/salt-pork.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Salt pork travels in sealed clay jars: a food, a trade good, and—quietly—a unit of account. People don’t just buy “pork”; they buy “two jars of winter cut,” and the seal on the lid matters as much as the meat inside.
Jars are honest in a cruel way. A broken jar is loss you can’t talk your way out of. A missing jar is theft that stinks on the hands. Whole districts in big cities live off the empty jars after the pork is long gone—grain storage, pickling, ash, nails, poor burials.
Common rumors

Inspectors can smell a resealed lid the way a priest can smell fear.
Old depots sometimes turn up with intact seals—either treasure, or trouble-by-brine.

See also

Pottery, Kilns, and Trade Seals
Banking Guild
City Watch

economy/saurakh.title: Saurakh
economy/saurakh.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Saurakh are the caravans’ quiet miracle: huge herbivorous reptiles built for heat, distance, and long days under a harness. A good saurakh team can haul a life’s worth of goods across bad roads without eating itself into bankruptcy. A panicked saurakh can turn a crowded street into a disaster before anyone finishes shouting.
They are heat-tolerant and most active in the day in desert regions, but in high-altitude cold they become nearly motionless to conserve warmth. In temperate parts of the Empire they can be pushed into night travel under duress, though handlers consider it bad practice.
Names you might hear

Trade/guild standard: Saurakh (plural Saurakhim)
Union civilian speech: Sauracco
Elven territories: Kethra
Desert tribes/caravans: Druun
Soldiers/mercenaries: Scale-mules

Common rumors

Saurakh refuse to cross Fey Roads unless blindfolded or drugged.
A spooked Saurakh can smell “wrongness in the air” before a mage can measure it.
Banking Guild couriers prefer Saurakh teams around warded cargo: they don’t panic the way horses do.

economy/sea-trade-routes.title: Sea Trade Routes
economy/sea-trade-routes.content:
What players would know
The sea is not a road. With three moons tugging at the world, tides argue with each other, currents migrate, and whole stretches of water become treacherous without warning. “Normal shipping” exists only as a story told by people who want investors.
Real routes are conditional: a certain moonrise, a certain season, a certain captain who survived it and hasn’t gone soft in the head. Merchants pay for tide-readers, priest-navigators, armed convoys, and insurance scribes who write contracts like prayers. Lose a route, and ports starve; hold one, and everyone suddenly has an opinion about your morals.
Common rumors

The safest lane this year won’t be the safest lane next year—don’t trust old charts.
Some captains swear the sea recognizes ships that have spilled refined magic.

See also

The Fey Roads
The Three-Moon Sea

economy/snake-blood-wine.title: Snake-Blood Wine
economy/snake-blood-wine.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Snake-blood wine is a Marcher frontier custom: strong wine or grain spirit
dosed with fresh snake blood, sometimes as dare, sometimes as medicine,
sometimes as ritual bravado. The Empire calls it barbaric; plenty of imperial
fools still try it in private.
Common rumors

The real stuff is taken hot, not bottled.
Half the Marches call it heritage. The other half call it boys showing off.

See also

The River Marches
Statesboro

economy/yage.title: Yage
economy/yage.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Yage is a controlled intoxicant made from dried, powdered black centipedes and
stabilizing binders. In small doses it loosens thought patterns; in heavy doses
it can scramble speech into fluent but unstable glossolalia.
It appears in three social lanes:

shamanic circles (ritualized, supervised),
orc research contexts (instrumental, measured),
undercity dens (recreational and often unsafe).

Common rumors

“Yage does not give prophecy; it strips the lies you tell yourself.”
“The first dose gives clarity. The third dose gives certainty. Certainty gets
people killed.”
“Bad batches make spell phrases drift just enough to fail at the worst
moment.”

economy/yellow-grass.title: Yellow Grass
economy/yellow-grass.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Yellow grass is the staple that keeps bellies full and borders worth fighting over. It bakes into pale bread, ferments into common beer, and hardens into travel rations that don’t rot as quickly as older grains. Where yellow grass grows well, people multiply; where it fails, politics turns sharp.
Farmers talk about it like it has moods. A cloudy summer can thin the harvest; a bad rotation can “tire the soil.” Caravans haul it by the sack and the jar, and monasteries keep careful stores because hunger makes heresy loud.
Common rumors

The yellow in the stalk is “stored sunlight,” and certain priests insist you can taste the season in the crust.
Some old families claim the elves taught the crop… and taught it to be dependent, too.

See also

Fish Farming
Insect Spice (Borrowed Heat)
Church Caravans
Sacrament Administration

environments/mountains-and-passes.title: Mountains and Passes
environments/mountains-and-passes.content:
What players would know
In Qualihut, mountains are not scenery. They are logistics that can kill you.
Passes open and close on weather, rockfall, and politics. A road that exists in summer can be a death sentence in winter. Old markers drift under snow, and “safe” routes become stories people trade with more fear than pride.
Those who live by the passes treat travel as a discipline: layered clothing, counted rations, witnessed route rights, and rules about fires, noise, and waste. The mountain doesn’t care what flag you carry. It only cares whether you know how to move.
Common rumors

The fastest way through a mountain is to follow someone who knows when not to go.
Some passes go quiet: no birds, no insects, no echo—just absence. That’s when you keep walking.

See also

Volcanic Faultlands
The Central Wilds

environments/old-growth-forests.title: Old-Growth Forests
environments/old-growth-forests.content:
What players would know
In the Empire, old-growth forests are not “wilderness.” They are politics.
The trees are protected, guarded, and argued over in courtrooms more often than they are cut. Wood is scarce in the places that matter, and logging is trouble—legal trouble, religious trouble, and sometimes the kind of trouble that has no paperwork.
Forests are also contested memory. Shrines appear where roads don’t, and certain groves are treated like borders: you can cross them, but only if you accept that you are being noticed.
Common rumors

Some forests are warded like vaults, and cutting the wrong tree counts as sacrilege.
The quickest way to start a feud is to accuse someone of wasteful felling.

See also

Pottery, Kilns, and Trade Seals
Salt Pork (Jar Trade)

environments/shifting-oases.title: Shifting Oases
environments/shifting-oases.content:
What players would know
In the desert, an oasis is not a town. It’s an appointment: water that agrees to be in one place for a while.
Because oases move, ownership is never comfortable. When multiple groups arrive at the same water, you get negotiation, withdrawal, or violence with rules—because the alternative is war that poisons the only thing everyone needs.
Common rumors

Some oases “shift” overnight after a tremor, leaving camps stranded with empty skins.
The smartest caravans arrive with witnesses, not just guards.

See also

The Desert (Living System)
The Travelers

environments/the-desert.title: The Desert (Living System)
environments/the-desert.content:
What players would know
The desert is not empty. It is unstable.
Water does not “run” here; it relocates. Oases appear, vanish, and migrate as if the land is changing its mind. A good map is a story you can trade, not a truth you can trust.
If you travel it, you learn quickly what the settled world forgets: permanence is a luxury. Routes are relationships. Waste is a crime. The desert punishes arrogance faster than violence.
What survives out there

Nomadic caravan-clans like the Travelers, who treat the road as law.
Herds of desert reptiles (beasts of burden, blood, and survival), and the Skyrider pairs who scout above the dunes.
Volcanic corridors and ash valleys, including the Eastern Passage, where rumor insists Ifrit keep the rules.

Common rumors

The desert produces a seasonal desert truffle that the Church quietly depends on.
Oases are “temporary courts”: when tribes collide, the fight has rules—or it becomes a war (Shifting Oases).

environments/the-three-moon-sea.title: The Three-Moon Sea
environments/the-three-moon-sea.content:
What players would know
The sea is not a road. With three moons tugging at the world, tides argue with each other, currents migrate, and “safe passage” is never permanent—only negotiated.
Ports live on conditional knowledge: this channel is passable this month, at this moonrise, if your captain knows the signs and your crew can stomach what they’ll see when the water decides to misbehave.
Common rumors

Old charts get people killed because they encourage confidence.
Monsters treat shipping lanes like feeding corridors.
Some priests can “hear” the tide the way others hear confession.

See also

Sea Trade Routes
The Three Moons

environments/three-moons.title: The Three Moons
environments/three-moons.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Qualihut has three moons, and the world behaves like it knows that. Tides argue. Sleep is not uniform. Magic has “good nights” and “bad nights” the way weather has fronts.
Most folk don’t track the whole sky. They track what matters to them:

Sailors care which moon is pulling hardest.
Midwives care which moon makes blood easy or stubborn.
Undertakers care which moon makes memory linger.

People argue about calendars, but agree on one thing: when the moons align strangely, the world gets soft in ways you can’t litigate.
Common rumors

One moon is always “high” (strong), one is fading, and one is quiet. The world is never neutral.
Triple alignment is rare and weird: births don’t fit lineage, vows bind too hard, and old stories walk around like they own the place.
Triple alignment comes about once in a lifetime—roughly every four decades—and every calendar lies about the exact week.
The Solar Church pretends its miracles ignore the moons. Everybody else plans around them.

See also

Elunara
The Three-Moon Sea

environments/volcanic-faultlands.title: Volcanic Faultlands
environments/volcanic-faultlands.content:
What players would know
The volcanic belt is the Empire’s reminder that the world is unfinished. Ash valleys cut trade in half. Vents open where roads used to be. Old lava tubes become smugglers’ dreams until they become tombs.
Most maps treat the faultlands as “blank” not because no one has looked, but because the terrain refuses permanence. People who travel near it learn to read the sky: not for weather, but for the color of the dust.
Common rumors

Some passages only exist for a season, then collapse like a bad promise.
Fire-willed beings—Ifrit—treat trespass as fuel.

See also

The Eastern Passage
Mountains & Passes

factions/banking-guild.title: Banking Guild
factions/banking-guild.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Banking Guild—formally Il Consorzio della Mano Sicura—is turning trust into infrastructure. Where old lords demanded coin, the Guild offers paper backed by vaults, seals, and a ritualized promise: your note can be redeemed, witnessed, and made real.
In cities with strong guild presence, promissory notes start to behave like a trade standard. Merchants stop weighing coin and start weighing reputation. In places without it, the notes are still just paper—until someone with a ledger and a militia decides they aren’t.
Common rumors

Guild vaults hold unusual reserves.
Debtors sometimes vanish into “administrative disputes.”

factions/brazen-pike-company.title: Brazen Pike Company
factions/brazen-pike-company.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Brazen Pike Company is a contract mercenary outfit that sells disciplined
escort work: caravan protection, checkpoint muscle, debt-collection security,
and short-term gate control when local militias are stretched thin.
They are known for clear rates, written witness logs, and not drinking while on
watch.
Common rumors

If the Brazen Pike banner is on a caravan, trouble usually finds softer prey.
Their quartermasters ask more questions than their captains.

factions/casa-dei-tre-spilli.title: La Casa dei Tre Spilli
factions/casa-dei-tre-spilli.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)


La Casa dei Tre Spilli is a small Niederstadt thieves’ guild wrapped in a
respectable-enough front: mending, discreet rooms, and staff who know when not to
remember faces. It is not rich enough to be elegant or brutal enough to be famous,
which is exactly why certain kinds of business like it.
Common rumors

If someone asks for the “third pin,” they are not talking about tailoring.
The House rents privacy by the hour and silence by the favor.

factions/covenant-of-the-long-road.title: The Covenant of the Long Road
factions/covenant-of-the-long-road.content:
What players would know
In the desert, a banner doesn’t feed you. A road does. The Covenant of the Long Road is spoken of as an oath made from routes, wells, and mutual obligation—less a nation than a promise that caravans can travel without being bled dry at every crossing.
To city ears, it sounds almost boring: water rights, safe passage, shared rules for camps and markets. To people who profit from chokepoints, it sounds like revolution in polite clothing.
Common rumors

A matriarch called “the Unifier” is getting tribes to speak with one voice.
The Covenant’s law is carried in songs that list wells like saints.

See also

The Travelers
The Desert (Living System)

factions/gesso-bianco.title: La Compagnia del Gesso Bianco
factions/gesso-bianco.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)


La Compagnia del Gesso Bianco is a thieves’ guild known for jobs that avoid
blood: burglary, pickpocketing, and fraud done with timing and paperwork instead
of open violence. They are associated with chalk marks on doorframes and market
posts, though no one agrees what the symbols actually mean.
In crowded districts, they are blamed for “clean losses”: coin pouches gone
without cut straps, lockboxes opened without broken hinges, and debt records
that change hands before the ink is dry.
Common rumors

They case neighborhoods by posing as copyists, clerks, and tally-runners.
If Gesso Bianco steals from you, you’ll notice three days later, not three seconds later.

factions/mano-fortunata.title: La Mano Fortunata
factions/mano-fortunata.content:
What players would know
La Mano Fortunata (“the Lucky Hand”) is spoken of as a patronage circle that
collects around games of chance: high stakes, private rooms, and people who always
seem to be winning at the right time. To most citizens, they’re a rumor with
money behind it.
Public footprint

The name most people recognize is The Ivory Wheel, a fashionable casino with discreet guards and expensive silence. (See: La Mano Fortunata Guildhouse (The Ivory Wheel Casino).)
Their influence is felt as invitations, introductions, and “luck” that looks like coordination.

Common rumors

Their “favored” can get an appointment anywhere that takes bribes.
Losing to them is worse than losing money.

See also

Thieves’ Guilds

factions/ponte-nero.title: La Compagnia del Ponte Nero
factions/ponte-nero.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

La Compagnia del Ponte Nero is what you hire when you need movement more than you need explanations. Publicly they’re pilgrimage-season logistics: stables, transport-animal exchange, guides who can thread a caravan through crowds without bloodshed.
They have a reputation for quiet competence—the kind that makes officials uneasy. Ponte Nero people look like ordinary workers until you watch them solve a problem in three gestures and one glance.
Common rumors

They can “find a route” when roads close.
Their ledgers are cleaner than their work.

factions/southern-union.title: The Southern Union
factions/southern-union.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Southern Union is a cluster of nations bound together by treaty and trade—close enough in strength to the Empire that open war would be ruinous for everyone, and therefore threatened constantly in speeches nobody intends to honor.
Union diplomats smile like merchants and argue like lawyers. In border taverns you hear two stories at once: that the Union is a civilized alternative to imperial feudal rot, and that the Union is a patient machine that prefers sabotage to banners.
Common rumors

“Union coin spends anywhere” (and Union promises spend twice).
If a monastery burns in the wilds, someone in the south will call it “self‑determination.”

factions/travelers.title: The Travelers
factions/travelers.content:
What players would know

People in settled lands call them “the Travelers” because it’s easier than learning the names of a dozen caravan-clans and their rules. They call themselves “the people who wander”. They move with the desert instead of against it: matriarchs bargain for water, routes, and shelter; caravans carry news like a living postal service; and their tents appear on the horizon like a mirage that decided to be practical.
To outsiders, they can look like smugglers, pilgrims, traders, or refugees depending on the day. To the Travelers, those are roles, not identities. What matters is whether you respect the road: how you take water, what you leave behind, and whether you keep your word when the map stops caring.
Society on the move

Caravan-clans, not a nation: a tribe is a moving network of tents, herds, debts, and witnesses. Membership is a web of obligation more than blood.
Matrilineal authority: matriarchs adjudicate water rights, route access, and feuds. They don’t command armies; they command permission.
Accounting as ethics: water is counted, grazing is negotiated, waste is punished. In desert law, carelessness is theft.

“The Tour” (coming-of-age wandering)
When a Traveler male comes of age, he is expected to leave his birth-group and travel—alone or in small bands—between tribes. This wandering is called the Tour. It is not exile; it is circulation.

Arrival without arrows: a Tourer who keeps the road-signs and approaches under the correct call is not attacked.
The matriarch’s test: the receiving matriarch sets a task. If he succeeds, he may be taken into the tribe’s web (by marriage, oath, or sponsorship). If he fails, he moves on with a story and a debt.
Those who don’t find a tribe often become the desert’s connective tissue in other forms: caravan hands, interpreters, city-runners, and “respectable” middlemen who can speak both sand and stone.

The sky-bonded
Tourers bond with a Skyrider: a flying desert reptile—a gliding, heat-loving hunter used as scout, courier, and omen. In settled lands, people often use “skyrider” to mean the bonded rider, the animal, or the pair; Travelers are more precise when it matters.
The bond is spoken of as telepathic in the way sailors speak of storms: not a metaphor, but a practical fact. A bonded pair can find each other across dunes, hold a course through dust that would blind a caravan, and sense danger before it has a shape.
Truffle harvest and sacrament rumors
In church and court, the polite story is that a desert truffle—harvested under strict seasonal constraints—is part of the Solar Church’s sacrament supply (Sacrament Administration). Most people don’t know whether the Travelers are the harvesters, the guardians, or merely the ones who can move it without it spoiling.
Oases and the politics of thirst
The desert’s oases are not towns. They are appointments—fleeting water in a landscape that refuses permanence. When multiple tribes converge on the same water, disputes turn into escalating violence or withdrawal to potential death by thirst.
The Eastern Passage and the Ifrit
There is an eastern route through volcanic country—the Eastern Passage—that outsiders call impossible. Travelers call it expensive. Stories say Ifrit keep it, and that caravans cross only by treaty, tribute, and the kind of promises that cannot be written down.
Common rumors

Their laws are older than the border stones, and harsher about waste than any city ordinance.
A Traveler caravan can guide you across the bad stretches… for a price that isn’t always coin.
Tourers who return with empty hands come back speaking like city clerks and sleeping like hunted animals.
The sky-riders can smell a well before a scout can see it.

See also

The Desert (Living System)
Shifting Oases
Desert Truffle
Desert Bamboo (Fast-Growth Trees)
Saurakh (Great Desert Reptiles)
Skyrider
The Eastern Passage
Ifrit

institutions/banco-valdieri.title: Banco Valdieri
institutions/banco-valdieri.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Banco Valdieri is one of Hochsilvar’s marble-faced certainties: reputable, wealthy, and guarded like a minor palace. It sits close to the Banking Guild’s promissory-note experiment, where paper promises are backed by refined magic and the public is asked to believe the ledgers.
If you want to know how much power a bank has, don’t look at its coin—look at who defers to it. Valdieri gets visits from guild representatives, court couriers, and people who never give their full names.
Common rumors

Their vaults hold “more than coin.”
A Valdieri account opens doors that shouldn’t open.

See also

Magister Argentum Alarich von Silberhain
Giovanni Valdieri

institutions/broadbarrel-caravan.title: The Broadbarrel Caravan
institutions/broadbarrel-caravan.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Broadbarrel Caravan is a slow, heavy staple convoy: salt pork jars, ale
kegs, and yellow-grass sacks hauled in bulk under strict schedules.
It is run by Henrik Volmar and currently
travels with hired Brazen Pike Company
security.
Common rumors

If you need food moved through bad country, Broadbarrel usually delivers.
Their guard contract is expensive enough to scare off petty trouble.

institutions/church-caravans.title: Church Caravans
institutions/church-caravans.content:
What players would know
Church caravans are the Solar Church on wheels: wagons under sun‑banners, guarded by armed devotees, carrying relic chests, sealed casks, and documents that become law once stamped in the right ink. When a church caravan rolls into a town, the market reorganizes itself around it. People line up for blessings, petitions, and rumors.
They travel with procedures as much as with cargo—inventories recited like prayers, handoffs performed as rituals, and enough witnesses to make theft feel like blasphemy. That doesn’t stop thieves; it just changes what they’re stealing.
Common rumors

Some caravans carry sacrament stock under double seals, and the seals are counted twice a day.
A caravan’s “paperwork wagon” is more heavily guarded than its gold.

institutions/city-watch.title: City Watch
institutions/city-watch.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

City Watch patrols keep order the way a tired person keeps a room clean: by deciding what mess is “normal.” They’re underpaid, stretched thin, and often more local than lawful—loyal to districts, captains, and survival.
Watch captains spend as much time balancing guild pressure against magistrate orders as they do chasing criminals. The result is uneven enforcement that looks like corruption to outsiders and looks like “not getting everyone killed” to the people doing the work.
Common rumors

A guild coin buys faster justice than a badge.
City watch units and guild enforcers skirmish after dark.

institutions/convergence-directorate.content:
What players would know

formed to restore magical reliability during periods of instability.
Publicly, it audits spell protocols, ward geometry, and cross-city calibration
rules.
Common rumors

Directorate mages can make five cities cast from one rulebook.
Their methods lower accident rates and raise political panic at the same
time.
Their best people are calm, precise, and increasingly hard to surprise.

institutions/cult-of-ink.title: The Cult of Ink
institutions/cult-of-ink.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Cult of Ink is spoken of in the same voice people use for plague and debt: low, practical, and a little superstitious. They are contract killers—allegedly neutral, allegedly precise, and allegedly bound by written terms so strict they will not “improvise mercy” even if begged.
In some cities, a small black droplet painted on a doorframe is enough to make a landlord suddenly decide to be reasonable. In others, it’s just a joke thieves tell each other. Either way, most people agree on one thing: if the Cult has your name in ink, the law won’t save you—only a better contract will.
Common rumors

They don’t take sides, only clauses.
Their tattoos are not decoration; they’re vows you can’t wash off.

institutions/der-kronenschild.title: Der Kronenschild
institutions/der-kronenschild.content:
What players would know
Der Kronenschild is the Empire’s internal continuity apparatus: the people who show up when a situation stops being a crime and becomes a threat to “harmony.” Officially they preserve stability and prevent sedition. Unofficially, they are famous for consequences delivered with impeccable manners.
If the City Watch is local law, Kronenschild is the Crown’s cross‑jurisdiction bureau: the seal that lets someone investigate across feudal boundaries and treat “a case” as a state problem.
Common rumors

They apologize while ruining your life.
If they “ask questions,” the verdict has already been filed.

institutions/der-sonnenmarsch.title: Der Sonnenmarsch
institutions/der-sonnenmarsch.content:
What players would know
Der Sonnenmarsch—“the Sun March”—is the Empire’s great pilgrimage season, when roads become rivers of people and faith turns into logistics. Merchants follow the pilgrims, pilgrims follow the banners, and everyone pretends the crowds are only about devotion and not about money, favors, and who gets to be seen walking close to the light.
The Church speaks of it as the Golden Walk: a chance to renew oaths, witness sanctioned miracles, and put your footsteps where your prayers have been pointing all year. City officials speak of it as a scheduling nightmare. Bandits speak of it as an opportunity, until they learn how many guards feel holy that week.
Common rumors

Every Sonnenmarsch has at least one “miracle” and at least one massacre—usually the same event, depending on where you stood.
If the march ever truly failed, people would still walk. That’s what scares the court.

institutions/der-weitblick.title: Der Weitblick
institutions/der-weitblick.content:
What players would know
Der Weitblick is the Empire’s “long-view” bureaucracy: offices of maps, trade reports, diplomatic notes, and threat assessments. Their public work is deliberately dull. When an institution insists it is only paper, people assume—often correctly—that the paper is the weapon.
Common rumors

They don’t start wars; they just make sure the timing is convenient.
If your name is in their files, you’ll never see the page.

institutions/doctrine-of-concord.title: Doctrine of Concord
institutions/doctrine-of-concord.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Doctrine of Concord is the Empire’s preferred language for explaining
itself: harmony through proper station, disciplined conduct, and competent
administration. Magistrates, clerks, and reformers cite it when they want power
to sound moral rather than merely strong.
Common rumors

Every frontier insult sounds gentler once somebody wraps it in Concord.
A clerk quoting Concord usually means your petition is about to become
paperwork.

See also

The River Marches

institutions/feudal-empire.title: Feudal Empire
institutions/feudal-empire.content:
What players would know
The Empire is vast, feudal, and uneven. Imperial edicts arrive late, if they arrive at all, and enforcement depends on who benefits. Most people experience “the Empire” as a set of tolls, a calendar of levies, and the occasional parade meant to remind everyone who owns the map.
Day-to-day power is local: lords, guilds, churches, mayors, caravan captains. The center claims authority; the edges negotiate it.
Common rumors

The Throne is weaker than the caravans.
Provincial keeps follow the emperor only when convenient.

institutions/hochkathedrale-der-ewigen-f.title: Die Hochkathedrale der Ewigen Flamme
institutions/hochkathedrale-der-ewigen-f.content:
What players would know
The High Cathedral of the Eternal Flame is the Solar Church’s crown of stone and light—part temple, part court, part machine for turning doctrine into enforceable reality. Pilgrims come to pray. Nobles come to be seen praying. Everyone else comes because the Cathedral’s decisions ripple outward into taxes, marriages, pardons, and wars.
Loyalists call it the Sun Crown. Common folk call it simply “the Flame,” as if naming it too fully would invite attention. Standing in its precinct feels like being watched by a beautiful idea that does not always care about people.
Common rumors

The Cathedral keeps archives that can unmake a noble house with a single page.
On certain feast days, the light inside falls at angles that make liars nauseous.

undercity waterworks, cistern access control, and tunnel logistics.
They sit at the junction of infrastructure control and subterranean politics.
Sigil (player-safe)

Common rumors

Nachtquell can flood a district by enforcing maintenance too literally.
Their cistern keys are more valuable than some crowns.

See also

Noble House Roster (Twenty Houses)

institutions/house-von-silberhain.title: House von Silberhain
institutions/house-von-silberhain.content:
What players would know
House von Silberhain is one of the Twenty Houses. It is most often associated with
wardcraft auditing, vault-binding expertise, and magical custody protocols.
They are treated as technical arbiters whenever institutions fight over magical evidence.
Sigil (player-safe)

Common rumors

Silberhain audits can ruin a bank faster than robbery.
If they say a seal held, everyone asks who satisfied it.

See also

Noble House Roster (Twenty Houses)

institutions/house-von-sonnenfels.title: House von Sonnenfels
institutions/house-von-sonnenfels.content:
What players would know
House von Sonnenfels is one of the Twenty Houses. It is most often associated with
imperial law theater, sacrament legitimacy, and succession arbitration.
Their public identity is closely tied to Althar and solar legal ritual.
Sigil (player-safe)

Common rumors

A Sonnenfels clerk can make a disputed heir look inevitable by sunset.
Their witnesses remember everything that helps the empire and little else.

See also

Noble House Roster (Twenty Houses)

institutions/house-von-stillwort.title: House von Stillwort
institutions/house-von-stillwort.content:
What players would know
House von Stillwort is an elven noble house known for immaculate restraint: soft voices, precise clothing, and the feeling that even their silences are practiced. In court they present as advisors, archivists, and “quiet overseers” whose influence arrives without spectacle and leaves people rearranging their lives around new procedures.
They are also the one house commonly associated with warlock power—not as a free-for-all talent, but as a lineage-bound inheritance tied to an ancestral bargain. In the popular telling, warlock power has manifested in their bloodline ever since.
Sigil (player-safe)

Common rumors

Their ancestor made a pact with an entity called The Silent Poet, and the debt still echoes in the bloodline.
Their warlocks are tolerated because they are useful—and watched because they are never fully trusted.
Their household teaches “restraint” like a martial art: when not to speak, when not to write, when not to remember.
Outsiders call them “the House of Warlocks,” usually when they think no one is listening.

institutions/house-von-weissdorn.title: House von Weissdorn
institutions/house-von-weissdorn.content:
What players would know
House von Weissdorn is one of the Twenty Houses. It is most often associated with
shrine estates, moon-calendric agriculture, and ritual hosting rights.
They bind agrarian timing, local devotion, and estate authority.
Sigil (player-safe)

Common rumors

Weissdorn almanacs can change planting behavior across provinces.
Their shrine festivals quietly settle local power balances.

See also

Noble House Roster (Twenty Houses)

institutions/imperial-monasteries.title: Imperial Monasteries
institutions/imperial-monasteries.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

Imperial monasteries sit where towns don’t: on dangerous roads, near old stones, and in valleys where the wind sounds like it’s remembering something. To travelers they’re refuge—warmth, bread, a place to sleep without a knife at your throat. To officials they’re outposts, record houses, and quiet points of influence beyond city walls.
Some monasteries are thriving, with gardens and disciplined hospitality. Others are half‑abandoned, still tended by a handful of stubborn monks who act like the world ending is just another chore. Either way, people speak of monasteries as places where you can ask for help… and where help always comes with a lesson.
Common rumors

Monks know which roads are “wrong” this season, even when maps insist they’re fine.
An abandoned monastery is never truly empty; it’s just between owners.

institutions/intelligence-bureaus.title: Intelligence Bureaus
institutions/intelligence-bureaus.content:
What players would know
Every power center keeps spies. Politics isn’t only speeches and votes; it’s sabotage, rumor campaigns, coerced witnesses, and disappearances politely attributed to bandits.
Most people can’t name the bureaus, only the symptoms: a rival’s caravan “misroutes,” a scandal breaks at the perfect time, a clerk loses the only copy of a document that mattered.
Common rumors

Assassins travel with caravans.
Magistrates hire thieves’ guilds for deniable jobs.

institutions/lamp-feeders-niederstadt.title: Lamp Feeders (Niederstadt Utility)
institutions/lamp-feeders-niederstadt.content:
What players would know
Illustration (player-safe)

The Lamp Feeders are Niederstadt’s municipal lighting crews. They maintain
caged bioluminescent beetles that light tunnels, stairs, and market approaches
through the undercity night.
Most residents barely notice them until a lane goes dim, a mugging spike
starts, or a district complains that “the lamps feel wrong.”
Common rumors

Rich lanes get brighter cages and fresher feed.
A feeder can read tunnel trouble by glow color before anyone files a report.
Smashing a lamp cage is stupid; culling quietly is how professionals make
darkness.

See also

Nieder Lamp Beetle

institutions/lineage-stewardship.title: Lineage Stewardship
institutions/lineage-stewardship.content:
What players would know
Elven noble houses treat family like a long project. Lineage stewards are the people who keep that project on track: genealogists, match‑brokers, physicians, and quiet advisors who talk about “harmony” the way generals talk about supply.
In polite company, stewardship is framed as care—preventing scandal, preserving health, arranging alliances. In rougher company, it’s framed as control. Human courtiers whisper about ledgers that track bloodlines across centuries and about children “sent away” to cloisters for reasons nobody will state plainly.
Common rumors

Some houses can predict a child’s temperament the way farmers predict weather.
A steward’s smile means you are being measured for a life you didn’t choose.

institutions/merchant-houses.title: Merchant Houses
institutions/merchant-houses.content:
What players would know
Merchant houses began as trade families and grew into institutions: buying council seats, funding militias, and shaping law with contracts instead of crowns. Their caravans keep provinces fed, supplied, and informed, which makes them indispensable to nobles who pretend to despise them.
In practice, a merchant seal can open doors a baron can’t—because the baron still needs flour to arrive.
Common rumors

A merchant’s seal is worth more than a baron’s.
Merchant houses purchase minor titles to dodge tariffs.

institutions/noble-house-roster.title: Noble House Roster (Twenty Houses)
institutions/noble-house-roster.content:
What players would know
Court clerks, card printers, and heralds often talk about the “Twenty Houses”:
the noble roster most commonly used for state ceremonies, betting decks, and
marriage politics. Different cities argue about rank order, but the names are
widely recognized.
The Twenty Houses (common register)

House von Dornfels
